intro: Arthur Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic recorded the first movement, Allegro con brio, of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, in 1913, playing into a recording horn. The exposition repeat is omitted, so the E♭-major second theme leads directly into the development, where the opening rhythm is broken into fragments.

sections.label: A · Opening motif in octaves
sections.mNote: Three short notes descend to a long note under a fermata.

sections.label: B · Horn call towards E♭
sections.mNote: A violin melody follows the horn call

sections.label: C · Development, horns and strings
sections.mNote: The development begins; D♭ in the strings clashes with G.

sections.label: D · Diminished chords, wind and strings
sections.mNote: Wind and strings alternate diminished chords before C minor returns.

sections.label: E · C-major cadences into the coda
sections.mNote: The long closing passage returns to C minor.

cues.title: Opening fermatas, bars 1–5
cues.text: Three Gs fall to E♭, then three Fs fall to D. Each long note has a fermata, which gave Nikisch room to hold the orchestra still. The second hold lasts across two written bars.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Acoustic recording, Berlin, 1913
cues.text: On 10 November 1913 Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic recorded the whole symphony in one day. The engineer Max Hampe captured their playing through a horn. Air moved a diaphragm, and a stylus cut the music into wax.
cues.evidence: Aleks Kolkowski, Duncan Miller and Amy Blier-Carruthers, ‘The art and science of acoustic recording’, Science Museum Group Journal, 2015: session, engineer and acoustic recording process. https://journal.sciencemuseum.ac.uk/article/acoustic-recording/

cues.title: Horn call before the violin melody
cues.text: The horns stretch the opening rhythm into a call across wider intervals. Their last B♭ is held beneath the violin melody, which begins softly in E♭ major. The cellos continue the repeated notes underneath.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–70; Mutopia 941, horns, first violin and cello.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Start of the development
cues.text: Nikisch left out the exposition repeat. After the E♭-major cadence, the horns’ three B♭s fall to G and the strings follow with D♭–D♭–D♭–C, which begins the development (bars 125–128).
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–128; Mutopia 941. The omitted repeat is documented by Kolkowski, Miller and Blier-Carruthers: https://journal.sciencemuseum.ac.uk/article/acoustic-recording/.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening motif
cues.text: G–G–G–E♭ returns, with winds and horns reinforcing the strings. Beethoven has rebuilt the opening from short fragments and quiet chord exchanges. The fermatas stop the orchestra again.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 233–253; Mutopia 941, strings, oboes and horns. The recapitulation begins at 248.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Oboe solo, bar 268
cues.text: A G-major chord stops the orchestra, but the oboe holds its note. Alone, it descends F–E♭–D, adds a turn and descends again. Beethoven writes Adagio over this short solo inside the Allegro.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe part and string rests.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Horn call in the bassoons
cues.text: The bassoons take over the horn call, now G–G–G–C–D–G. The violin melody follows in C major. Its first leap, G up to C, keeps the shape of the earlier version and brings the melody closer to the home key.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and first-violin parts; compare 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bass line under a held C
cues.text: The violins hold a high C while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F, so the cadence does not close here. The coda ends later with its closing chords in C minor.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381 and 491–502; Mutopia 941, string parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
